signals.title: prevent infinity waiting on remote DC in multiregional mode when failover #12071
signals.text: ### Commit 1: XDB-546 — Show keys data size and moving size when DD is initializing File: `fdbserver/clustercontroller/Status.cpp` __What:__ Moved the "DD is initializing" early-return check __after__ parsing `dataStats`, so that partition count, moving data size, and other data metrics are still populated in the status JSON even during DD initialization. Previously, these fields were omitted because the function returned before parsing them. __Why:__ To show moving-data volume during DD initialization (e.g., after a failover) instead of waiting for initialization to complete. --- ### Commit 2: XDB-546 — Add degraded multiregion status when recovery is stuck at accepting_commits __Files:__ `fdbserver/clustercontroller/Status.cpp`, `fdbclient/Schemas.cpp`, `fdbcli/StatusCommand.cpp` __What:__ 1. Introduced a `degraded_multi_region` flag: set to `true` when the cluster is configured with `usableRegions > 1` and recovery is stuck at `accepting_commits`. Exposed this field in the status JSON schema. 2. When DD reports its state as `initializing` in a degraded multiregion scenario, the description now reads `"Degraded multiregional (Re)initializing automatic data distribution"` — making the nature of the degradation explicit. 3. In `fdbcli status` output, when `degraded_multi_region` is `true`, the warning message *"may have data loss and availability loss"* is suppressed. This is replaced with a neutral header followed by the actionable message (which TLog interfaces to restart). __Why:__ In a multi-region cluster, when one region fails, recovery gets stuck at `accepting_commits` because the failed region's logs are unreachable. However, commits are already being accepted in the surviving region (and its satellite), and all committed data is safe and consistent. This is a __degraded-but-not-data-losing__ state. Previously, `fdbcli status` showed a misleading warning about potential data loss. Now the status honestly reflects degraded multiregion without a false data-loss alarm. topic in foundationdb forum about this problem : [link](https://forums.foundationdb.org/t/3dc2regions-simulating-primary-datacenter-failure/3329/5)

signals.title: fixed unability to run more than one commit proxy in small configurations
signals.text: Rebase PR https://github.com/apple/foundationdb/pull/10411 Co-authored-by: @oleg68 Oleg Samarin [osamarin@openintegration.inc] # Fixed unability to run more than one commit proxy in small configurations ## Problem statement By default, the desired nubrer of commit proxies is 3. But in small configurations with 3 stateless processes (and any number of transaction and storage processes) foundationdb runs only one commit proxy process, that may cause some performance issues with high write volume. Any attempts to change the number of proxies with `configure commit_proxies=2` and so on do not help: it change only the ``Desired commit proxies`` value shown by the `status` fdbcli command, but *do not change* the actual number of commit proxies. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Create an FDB cluster 2. Setup three stateless server, processes and, for example, three transaction and three storage processes 3. Execute ``fdbcli --exec "status json" | grep commit_proxy`` ## Expected result Three lines ``` "role" : "commit_proxy" "role" : "commit_proxy" "role" : "commit_proxy" ``` ## Actual result Only one line ``` "role" : "commit_proxy" ``` ## Findings As far as I understand a list of worker candidates is determined by the `ClusterControllerData::getWorkersForRoleInDatacenter` method. The reason why it doesn't return more than one worker is the condition ``id_used[it.first] <= minWorker.get().used`` that is never satisfied with small number of stateless processes. ## Proposal 1. Fill out the worker candidate list `fitness_workers` regardless how much they are used. 2. Fill out the result worker list with desired number of workers with the lowerst usage count. Proposed PR implements these ideas. It - introduces the `used_fitness` local variable that is filled by the lowest fitness value of availdable processes - addes filtering by `used_fitness` when the result list is filled to use only workers with the smallest fitness value - eliminates the condition ``id_used[it.first] <= minWorker.get().used`` After applying this PR all desired number of commit proxies is recruited as long as there is a sufficient number number of stateless processes.

signals.title: Plumb TraceID/SpanID into debug tracing logs
signals.text: I found that debug transactions offer the highest quality telemetry for where in the commit pipeline a transaction gets stuck, but that the logs were difficult to work with (need to join across log lines distributed across roles to get the full connected graph of IDs that belong to a debug transaction). The tracing tool we use internally does not support this kind of stateful aggregation and instead relies on a consistent TraceID plumbed throughout the call graph. Conveniently, this already exists in the code base in the form of the OTEL tracing context. I added those IDs to all debug logs and was able to get a trace view in our systems that is useful to me. Here's what it looks like in our internal trace viewing tool. Yellow boxes correspond to the FDB Client debug traces (NativeAPIActor), the smaller green events are coming from GRV, Commit, and Storage Servers. This gives me a good view of stalls anywhere in the transaction lifecycle. I'm still refining how I parse these to make them more visually intuitive, but already useful in its current state. I use this by setting the Transaction ID through the SpecialKeys API, which then sets the span context: ```java String debugTransactionId = getDebugTransactionIdFromTraceMetadata(traceMetadata); String specialKeysTransactionId = getFdbTransactionIdFromTraceMetadata(traceMetadata); log.debug( "Enabling FDB transaction debugging", SafeArg.of("debugTransactionId", debugTransactionId), SafeArg.of("specialKeysTransactionId", specialKeysTransactionId)); transaction.options().setSpecialKeySpaceEnableWrites(); transaction.set(FDB_TRACING_TRANSACTION_ID_KEY, specialKeysTransactionId.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); transaction.options().setDebugTransactionIdentifier(debugTransactionId); transaction.options().setLogTransaction(); transaction.options().setServerRequestTracing(); ```

signals.title: Add ipv6 support to docker container
signals.text: Added functionality for `fdb.bash` to support ipv6, provided the new env variable `FDB_IP_VERSION` is set to 6 (or any string containing 6, such as v6, ipv6, iwantipv6, etc. ) There is an unfortunate caveat of no dual stack support, as FDB coordinators are recognized by their IP+port and not their machineid, to the best of my knowledge. If I'm wrong and FDB does not double count a coordinator with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in the cluster file, I would be happy to add dual stack support to this. This was part of now-split-up #13822, with slightly more robust logic. # Changes ## IPv6 Support ### Issue Before now, `fdb.bash` would throw an error if `hostname -i` resolved to a v6 address, as it would not be encased in brackets. ### New Behavior Depending on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, `fdb.bash` will try and find the machine's v4 or v6 address. IPv4 is the default pick. If `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` or `FDB_LISTEN_IP` are set, they will _not_ be overwritten. Otherwise, the first IPv4 (or IPv6, depending) address returned by `hostname -I` is used. This is used because under some dual stack networking setups (especially under Podman, looking at you pasta), only the v4 address will be written to `/etc/hosts`. At this point, if `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` still isn't set, an error is thrown that no valid IP could be found. `hostname -I` doesn't output a stable order, but containers often will only have a single IP address. In a container connected to multiple networks, there isn't a sure way to figure out the correct public IP automatically, which is why `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` isn't overwritten. ## Enhanced FDB_COORDINATOR ip resolution ### Issue FDB Coordinator discovery always looks up IPv4 addresses, as `dig` by default searches for A records. It also doesn't respect the local `/etc/hosts` file. ### New Behavior Based on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, fdb coordinator ip is discovered with either `getent ahostsv4` or `getent ahostsv6`. This will prefer the local hosts file if it has the name, otherwise it will try to reach a remote DNS server.

signals.title: BulkLoad: only require file containment for the range this fetchKeys owns
signals.text: A bulkload fetchKeys was rejecting the SST ingest fast path whenever any file in its task set fell outside the range being fetched, and falling back to key-value replay for the whole batch causing bulkload to take longer. The mismatch is structural, not a fault: two different range granularities meet in fetchKeys. bulkLoadFetchKeyValueFileToLoad builds localBulkLoadFileSets from the whole *task*, while `keys` is one destination shard piece. startMoveShards cuts the destination at pre-existing keyServers boundaries, so a task spanning several of them becomes several fetches -- and every one of those fetches is handed the task's entire file set, most of which belongs to the other pieces. Classifying all 3,428 mismatches on a 1B-key restore by how the offending file sits against the range being fetched: 87.0% no overlap 54.9% disjoint, 32.1% touching a boundary only 13.0% partial overlap 10.3% straddling an edge, 2.7% spanning it The 87% are not this fetch's files at all, so it can drop them and still ingest. Only the 13% are real conflicts -- ingesting those would write outside the range -- and they must still force the fallback. The all-or-nothing check was a deliberate guard, not an oversight: ingestSSTFiles was unfiltered, so ingesting a set containing unowned files would have written keys outside the shard. Fix the guard rather than remove it -- selectOwnedBulkLoadFileSets() keeps only the file sets whose range this fetch owns, and the fast path is then taken for those. Files that straddle or span a boundary still force the fallback, because ingesting them would write outside the range. selectOwnedBulkLoadFileSets() is pure and unit tested, including the exactly-once invariant: every file set must be claimed by exactly one fetch across the task's pieces, since dropping one silently loses data and duplicating one ingests the same keys twice. The test was confirmed red against the old behaviour (3 == 1). Measured effect on SSBulkLoadFileRangeMismatch at 100M scale: 342 before, then 85 and 199 in two later runs whose bulkload path was byte-identical. So the direction is established but the magnitude is not -- that counter has at least 2.3x run-to-run spread, driven by shard geometry rather than by this code. Also demote DDBulkLoadTaskFallbackToNormalDataMove from SevWarn to SevInfo. All 654 occurrences in the same run were Reason=PhaseMismatch on tasks already in phase Complete, at rebalance priorities 120 and 122 and never at the bulkload priority of 140. It is a benign race between a rebalance data move and task completion, not a bulkload fallback, and at SevWarn it was read as evidence of one. The attached task phase is deliberately not logged: it is a snapshot from when the task was Triggered/Running and can never show the Complete that caused the mismatch, which getBulkLoadTask already logs at SevWarn. ` 20260813-204050-stack_restore-bf06cb6ae1c0cb07 compressed=True data_size=38566706 duration=3617644 ended=100000 fail_fast=10 max_runs=100000 pass=100000 priority=100 remaining=0 runtime=0:27:55 sanity=False started=100000 stopped=20260813-210845 submitted=20260813-204050 timeout=5400 username=stack_restore`

signals.title: [release-7.4] Fix an old exclude failed bug
signals.text: Port apple/foundationdb#13645 to release-7.4. Problem: In removeKeysFromFailedServer, the writes that unassign a dropped shard from the dest servers (serverKeysFalse) and the writes that reassign it to the new team as an empty range were pushed into a single actors vector and awaited together. krmSetRangeCoalescing performs a read-modify-write on the serverKeys map, so when a server appears in both the dest set and the new team, running the two batches concurrently lets the coalescing reads observe stale state and produce an incorrect serverKeys assignment. Solution: await the unassign batch first, then run the empty-range assignment in a separate batch, ensuring the serverKey map assignment is correct. Same fix already backported to release-7.3 in apple/foundationdb#13662. release-7.4 still used the wait()/actor-compiler style rather than main's co_await, and shardId needed to become state since it now crosses the new wait() boundary -- same conflict resolution as the 7.3 backport. 100K: 20260813-171407-praza-port-7.4-pr13645-817f-e3951c728b485de6 pass=100000 fail=0 ended=100000 max_runs=100000

signals.text: Simplify the googlebenchmark download and compile by switching from `ExternalProject_Add()` with additional custom cmake `execute_process()` commands, to `FetchContent_Declare()` + `_MakeAvailable()` The motivation was to more easily and cleanly fix compile errors on recent macOS with recent clang+libcxx, which automatically enable warning option `-Wthread-safety-analysis` which is not compatible with this library and fails the build if `-Werror` is enabled: googlebenchmark-download/googlebenchmark-src/src/mutex.h:79:40: error: mutex 'mut_' is still held at the end of function [-Werror,-Wthread-safety-analysis] 79 | void lock() ACQUIRE() { mut_.lock(); } | ^ (The default "all" ninja target does not pull in googlebenchmark, but the "packages" and "strip_targets" ninja targets do, and I haven't been able to build them on my local recent macOS before. In CI we use macOS 14.x still which has older clang/libcxx and does not have the thread-safety analysis feature.) It seemed like the cleanest way of avoiding this build error was to ensure `-Werror` is disabled for googlebenchmark, and the best way to do that was to cleanup the googlebenchmark build. signals.title: Audit: bound validate_restore's slowest task instead of its average batch
signals.text: The `validate_restore` audit phase finishes only when its slowest task does, and nothing bounded that task. Measured at 100M scale, the slowest task took **2535.86s of a 2536.0s phase — 100% of the wall clock**, so per-task throughput improvements could not move the phase at all. An earlier attempt raised the per-batch byte budget, gained a real 1.94x in per-task throughput and a 25% lower median, and made the phase **25% slower**, because that run's shards happened to be 1.87x fatter. It was optimising an average when the metric is a maximum. ## `Audit: bound validate_restore's slowest task instead of its average batch` Three changes, in the order they matter: 1. **Cap the size of one audit task.** `scheduleAuditOnRange` divided work by live `keyServers` boundaries — one task per shard, dispatched to a single storage server that scans it sequentially — with no size cap anywhere in the audit dispatch path, so a fat shard was an unbounded straggler. Shards above `AUDIT_TASK_MAX_BYTES` (default 128MB) are now subdivided via `splitStorageMetrics`, lazily one shard at a time so the first task dispatches immediately. A failed metrics read falls back to the unsplit shard — the previous behaviour — so this cannot fail an audit that would otherwise pass. `minSplitBytes` is deliberately `target/8`, not the target: the storage server stops splitting once `remaining.bytes < 2 * minSplitBytes`, so passing the target refuses a split to every shard below twice the target. Measured with that mistake in place, 287 of 867 tasks sat unsplit in the 128–256MB band and the tail stayed at 1215.92s. 2. **Treat the batch byte budget as a ceiling and adapt within it.** `AUDIT_RESTORE_BATCH_BYTE_LIMIT` previously used `CLIENT_KNOBS->REPLY_BYTE_LIMIT` (80KB), a generic per-RPC-reply cap roughly 1750x tighter than `AUDIT_RESTORE_BATCH_KEY_LIMIT`, so raising the key limit had no effect. Raising it to a fixed 4MB tripled `transaction_too_old` (679 → 2515), because a batch too large for current conditions overruns its read transaction and the retry re-reads the same range — oversized batches buy double work, not throughput. The budget now halves on a retryable error and increases additively on success, between `AUDIT_RESTORE_BATCH_BYTE_LIMIT_MIN` and the ceiling. Cluster conditions vary between runs by more than the effect being tuned for, so a hand-tuned constant is fast on a good day and storms on a bad one. Retries also slept a flat 1.0s regardless of cause — pure latency when the remedy is a smaller batch, and one server logged 1,610 retries in a single audit. They now back off geometrically from 50ms to `AUDIT_RESTORE_RETRY_BACKOFF_MAX`. And `numValidatedKeys`/`validatedBytes` were accumulated *before* the progress-persist and rate-limiter waits that can throw, so every retried batch double-counted the very counters the throughput analysis reads; they are now snapshotted and rolled back. 3. **Let a server work several audit tasks at once.** `SERVE_AUDIT_STORAGE_PARALLELISM` defaulted to 1, so subdivided pieces landing on the same server would serialize and the cap would buy nothing; the default is now 4. This affects default deployments only — any configuration already overriding the knob is unchanged. That made the rate limiter's scope wrong: three call sites each built their own `SpeedLimit`, so concurrent tasks multiplied an allowance whose knob is named `AUDIT_STORAGE_RATE_PER_SERVER_MAX`. One limiter is now shared per server, and time blocked on it is reported in `SSAuditRestoreComplete` — `auditRestoreQ` had no limiter accounting at all, so a throttled audit was indistinguishable from a slow one. ## Two report-storm fixes - **`BulkLoad: report a failed task once, not on every metadata rescan`** — `scheduleBulkLoadTasks()` rescans task metadata every `DD_BULKLOAD_SCHEDULE_MIN_INTERVAL_SEC`, and a task in the terminal `Error` phase is deliberately left in place (unlike `Acknowledged`, it is never erased), so the `SevWarnAlways` report fired again on every scan for the life of the cluster. - **`BulkDump: warn on a task giving up, not on every retry attempt`** — the SS bulkdump loop retries up to 50 times, a second apart, while shards move underneath it; retrying is the normal path. Every attempt logged `SevWarn SSBulkDumpError`, so one task could emit fifty warnings naming an error it recovered from. Both matter beyond tidiness: this is how the real failure ends up buried thousands of log lines from the top. ## Results Measured at 100M (audit phase, same harness and dataset): | | before | after | |---|---|---| | audit phase | 42m16s | **25m00s** (also 26% below the 33m47s pre-existing baseline) | | `transaction_too_old` | 2515 | **150** (below the baseline's 679) | | aggregate audit throughput | 79 MB/s | **130 MB/s** | | `RateLimiterTotalWaitTime` | — | 0, so the shared limiter never bound | Zero `SSAuditRestoreError`, zero `StorageServerFailed`. These numbers were taken with the `minSplitBytes` mistake described above still present, so they understate the tail improvement. ## Testing Two pure helpers carry unit tests, both confirmed red before the fix: `auditTaskRangesFromSplitPoints()` for the property that pieces tile the input range exactly once (a gap leaves bytes unaudited while still reporting success; an overlap double-audits and writes conflicting progress metadata), and `nextAuditBatchBytes()` for the property that the budget stays within `[floor, ceiling]` and never reaches zero (a zero budget turns the batch loop into endless empty reads). `boundAuditTaskRange()` is covered by a mock that also asserts `minSplitBytes <= target/2`, because that defect is silent — subdivision just does not happen and the only symptom is a slower tail that looks like variance. Per-batch traces are gated behind the existing `ENABLE_AUDIT_VERBOSE_TRACE` knob, matching how `DataDistribution.cpp` already treats its audit traces; at 1B scale they were ~18M unconditional `SevInfo` events. ` 20260817-231125-stack-13886-92efb74f81420436 compressed=True data_size=38664449 duration=3545895 ended=100000 fail_fast=10 max_runs=100000 pass=100000 priority=100 remaining=0 runtime=0:31:52 sanity=False started=100000 stopped=20260817-234317 submitted=20260817-231125 timeout=5400 username=stack-13886 `

signals.title: Retry old-epoch backup mutation-log uploads
signals.text: ## Summary An I/O error while writing partitioned backup logs can terminate an old-epoch backup worker. Those failures deliberately do not restart transaction recovery, so the old log generation can remain retained and backup progress can stop indefinitely. Retry `io_error` and `io_timeout` for old-epoch mutation-log uploads while retaining the same role and message prefix. Each attempt opens fresh files. Freeze the recipient ranges and encoding boundaries so an ambiguous finish produces byte-identical duplicates, and handle newly observed overlapping backups before discarding messages or advancing durable progress. Add focused regression coverage for file creation, partial append, ambiguous finish, changing recipients, long transient outages, and stopping during an upload or retry. ## Validation - `fdbserver_backupworker_test`: 8/8 in normal mode and 8/8 in simulation mode. - `BackupCorrectnessPartitioned.toml` with buggify and fault injection enabled: passed; backup and restore completed. - A matched control with only old-epoch retries disabled reproduces the stalled backup; enabling retries completes the same test. - The workload and fault settings are unchanged. signal.title: fixed unability to run more than one commit proxy in small configurations
signal.text: Rebase PR https://github.com/apple/foundationdb/pull/10411 Co-authored-by: @oleg68 Oleg Samarin [osamarin@openintegration.inc] # Fixed unability to run more than one commit proxy in small configurations ## Problem statement By default, the desired nubrer of commit proxies is 3. But in small configurations with 3 stateless processes (and any number of transaction and storage processes) foundationdb runs only one commit proxy process, that may cause some performance issues with high write volume. Any attempts to change the number of proxies with `configure commit_proxies=2` and so on do not help: it change only the ``Desired commit proxies`` value shown by the `status` fdbcli command, but *do not change* the actual number of commit proxies. ## Steps to reproduce 1. Create an FDB cluster 2. Setup three stateless server, processes and, for example, three transaction and three storage processes 3. Execute ``fdbcli --exec "status json" | grep commit_proxy`` ## Expected result Three lines ``` "role" : "commit_proxy" "role" : "commit_proxy" "role" : "commit_proxy" ``` ## Actual result Only one line ``` "role" : "commit_proxy" ``` ## Findings As far as I understand a list of worker candidates is determined by the `ClusterControllerData::getWorkersForRoleInDatacenter` method. The reason why it doesn't return more than one worker is the condition ``id_used[it.first] <= minWorker.get().used`` that is never satisfied with small number of stateless processes. ## Proposal 1. Fill out the worker candidate list `fitness_workers` regardless how much they are used. 2. Fill out the result worker list with desired number of workers with the lowerst usage count. Proposed PR implements these ideas. It - introduces the `used_fitness` local variable that is filled by the lowest fitness value of availdable processes - addes filtering by `used_fitness` when the result list is filled to use only workers with the smallest fitness value - eliminates the condition ``id_used[it.first] <= minWorker.get().used`` After applying this PR all desired number of commit proxies is recruited as long as there is a sufficient number number of stateless processes.

It was optimising an average when the metric is a maximum. ## `Audit: bound validate_restore's slowest task instead of its average batch` Three changes, in the order they matter: 1. **Cap the size of one audit task.** `scheduleAuditOnRange` divided work by live `keyServers` boundaries — one task per shard, dispatched to a single storage server that scans it sequentially — with no size cap anywhere in the audit dispatch path, so a fat shard was an unbounded straggler. Shards above `AUDIT_TASK_MAX_BYTES` (default 128MB) are now subdivided via `splitStorageMetrics`, lazily one shard at a time so the first task dispatches immediately. A failed metrics read falls back to the unsplit shard — the previous behaviour — so this cannot fail an audit that would otherwise pass. `minSplitBytes` is deliberately `target/8`, not the target: the storage server stops splitting once `remaining.bytes < 2 * minSplitBytes`, so passing the target refuses a split to every shard below twice the target. Measured with that mistake in place, 287 of 867 tasks sat unsplit in the 128–256MB band and the tail stayed at 1215.92s. 2. **Treat the batch byte budget as a ceiling and adapt within it.** `AUDIT_RESTORE_BATCH_BYTE_LIMIT` previously used `CLIENT_KNOBS->REPLY_BYTE_LIMIT` (80KB), a generic per-RPC-reply cap roughly 1750x tighter than `AUDIT_RESTORE_BATCH_KEY_LIMIT`, so raising the key limit had no effect. Raising it to a fixed 4MB tripled `transaction_too_old` (679 → 2515), because a batch too large for current conditions overruns its read transaction and the retry re-reads the same range — oversized batches buy double work, not throughput. The budget now halves on a retryable error and increases additively on success, between `AUDIT_RESTORE_BATCH_BYTE_LIMIT_MIN` and the ceiling. Cluster conditions vary between runs by more than the effect being tuned for, so a hand-tuned constant is fast on a good day and storms on a bad one. Retries also slept a flat 1.0s regardless of cause — pure latency when the remedy is a smaller batch, and one server logged 1,610 retries in a single audit. They now back off geometrically from 50ms to `AUDIT_RESTORE_RETRY_BACKOFF_MAX`. And `numValidatedKeys`/`validatedBytes` were accumulated *before* the progress-persist and rate-limiter waits that can throw, so every retried batch double-counted the very counters the throughput analysis reads; they are now snapshotted and rolled back. 3. **Let a server work several audit tasks at once.** `SERVE_AUDIT_STORAGE_PARALLELISM` defaulted to 1, so subdivided pieces landing on the same server would serialize and the cap would buy nothing; the default is now 4. This affects default deployments only — any configuration already overriding the knob is unchanged. That made the rate limiter's scope wrong: three call sites each built their own `SpeedLimit`, so concurrent tasks multiplied an allowance whose knob is named `AUDIT_STORAGE_RATE_PER_SERVER_MAX`. One limiter is now shared per server, and time blocked on it is reported in `SSAuditRestoreComplete` — `auditRestoreQ` had no limiter accounting at all, so a throttled audit was indistinguishable from a slow one. ## Two report-storm fixes - **`BulkLoad: report a failed task once, not on every metadata rescan`** — `scheduleBulkLoadTasks()` rescans task metadata every `DD_BULKLOAD_SCHEDULE_MIN_INTERVAL_SEC`, and a task in the terminal `Error` phase is deliberately left in place (unlike `Acknowledged`, it is never erased), so the `SevWarnAlways` report fired again on every scan for the life of the cluster. - **`BulkDump: warn on a task giving up, not on every retry attempt`** — the SS bulkdump loop retries up to 50 times, a second apart, while shards move underneath it; retrying is the normal path. Every attempt logged `SevWarn SSBulkDumpError`, so one task could emit fifty warnings naming an error it recovered from. Both matter beyond tidiness: this is how the real failure ends up buried thousands of log lines from the top. ## Results Measured at 100M (audit phase, same harness and dataset): | | before | after | |---|---|---| | audit phase | 42m16s | **25m00s** (also 26% below the 33m47s pre-existing baseline) | | `transaction_too_old` | 2515 | **150** (below the baseline's 679) | | aggregate audit throughput | 79 MB/s | **130 MB/s** | | `RateLimiterTotalWaitTime` | — | 0, so the shared limiter never bound | Zero `SSAuditRestoreError`, zero `StorageServerFailed`. These numbers were taken with the `minSplitBytes` mistake described above still present, so they understate the tail improvement. ## Testing Two pure helpers carry unit tests, both confirmed red before the fix: `auditTaskRangesFromSplitPoints()` for the property that pieces tile the input range exactly once (a gap leaves bytes unaudited while still reporting success; an overlap double-audits and writes conflicting progress metadata), and `nextAuditBatchBytes()` for the property that the budget stays within `[floor, ceiling]` and never reaches zero (a zero budget turns the batch loop into endless empty reads). `boundAuditTaskRange()` is covered by a mock that also asserts `minSplitBytes <= target/2`, because that defect is silent — subdivision just does not happen and the only symptom is a slower tail that looks like variance. Per-batch traces are gated behind the existing `ENABLE_AUDIT_VERBOSE_TRACE` knob, matching how `DataDistribution.cpp` already treats its audit traces; at 1B scale they were ~18M unconditional `SevInfo` events. ` 20260817-231125-stack-13886-92efb74f81420436 compressed=True data_size=38664449 duration=3545895 ended=100000 fail_fast=10 max_runs=100000 pass=100000 priority=100 remaining=0 runtime=0:31:52 sanity=False started=100000 stopped=20260817-234317 submitted=20260817-231125 timeout=5400 username=stack-13886 `

signal.title: prevent infinity waiting on remote DC in multiregional mode when failover #12071
signal.text: ### Commit 1: XDB-546 — Show keys data size and moving size when DD is initializing File: `fdbserver/clustercontroller/Status.cpp` __What:__ Moved the "DD is initializing" early-return check __after__ parsing `dataStats`, so that partition count, moving data size, and other data metrics are still populated in the status JSON even during DD initialization. Previously, these fields were omitted because the function returned before parsing them. __Why:__ To show moving-data volume during DD initialization (e.g., after a failover) instead of waiting for initialization to complete. --- ### Commit 2: XDB-546 — Add degraded multiregion status when recovery is stuck at accepting_commits __Files:__ `fdbserver/clustercontroller/Status.cpp`, `fdbclient/Schemas.cpp`, `fdbcli/StatusCommand.cpp` __What:__ 1. Introduced a `degraded_multi_region` flag: set to `true` when the cluster is configured with `usableRegions > 1` and recovery is stuck at `accepting_commits`. Exposed this field in the status JSON schema. 2. When DD reports its state as `initializing` in a degraded multiregion scenario, the description now reads `"Degraded multiregional (Re)initializing automatic data distribution"` — making the nature of the degradation explicit. 3. In `fdbcli status` output, when `degraded_multi_region` is `true`, the warning message *"may have data loss and availability loss"* is suppressed. This is replaced with a neutral header followed by the actionable message (which TLog interfaces to restart). __Why:__ In a multi-region cluster, when one region fails, recovery gets stuck at `accepting_commits` because the failed region's logs are unreachable. However, commits are already being accepted in the surviving region (and its satellite), and all committed data is safe and consistent. This is a __degraded-but-not-data-losing__ state. Previously, `fdbcli status` showed a misleading warning about potential data loss. Now the status honestly reflects degraded multiregion without a false data-loss alarm. topic in foundationdb forum about this problem : [link](https://forums.foundationdb.org/t/3dc2regions-simulating-primary-datacenter-failure/3329/5)

signal.title: Plumb TraceID/SpanID into debug tracing logs
signal.text: I found that debug transactions offer the highest quality telemetry for where in the commit pipeline a transaction gets stuck, but that the logs were difficult to work with (need to join across log lines distributed across roles to get the full connected graph of IDs that belong to a debug transaction). The tracing tool we use internally does not support this kind of stateful aggregation and instead relies on a consistent TraceID plumbed throughout the call graph. Conveniently, this already exists in the code base in the form of the OTEL tracing context. I added those IDs to all debug logs and was able to get a trace view in our systems that is useful to me. Here's what it looks like in our internal trace viewing tool. Yellow boxes correspond to the FDB Client debug traces (NativeAPIActor), the smaller green events are coming from GRV, Commit, and Storage Servers. This gives me a good view of stalls anywhere in the transaction lifecycle. I'm still refining how I parse these to make them more visually intuitive, but already useful in its current state. I use this by setting the Transaction ID through the SpecialKeys API, which then sets the span context: ```java String debugTransactionId = getDebugTransactionIdFromTraceMetadata(traceMetadata); String specialKeysTransactionId = getFdbTransactionIdFromTraceMetadata(traceMetadata); log.debug( "Enabling FDB transaction debugging", SafeArg.of("debugTransactionId", debugTransactionId), SafeArg.of("specialKeysTransactionId", specialKeysTransactionId)); transaction.options().setSpecialKeySpaceEnableWrites(); transaction.set(FDB_TRACING_TRANSACTION_ID_KEY, specialKeysTransactionId.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); transaction.options().setDebugTransactionIdentifier(debugTransactionId); transaction.options().setLogTransaction(); transaction.options().setServerRequestTracing(); ```

signal.title: Add ipv6 support to docker container
signal.text: Added functionality for `fdb.bash` to support ipv6, provided the new env variable `FDB_IP_VERSION` is set to 6 (or any string containing 6, such as v6, ipv6, iwantipv6, etc. ) There is an unfortunate caveat of no dual stack support, as FDB coordinators are recognized by their IP+port and not their machineid, to the best of my knowledge. If I'm wrong and FDB does not double count a coordinator with both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses in the cluster file, I would be happy to add dual stack support to this. This was part of now-split-up #13822, with slightly more robust logic. # Changes ## IPv6 Support ### Issue Before now, `fdb.bash` would throw an error if `hostname -i` resolved to a v6 address, as it would not be encased in brackets. ### New Behavior Depending on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, `fdb.bash` will try and find the machine's v4 or v6 address. IPv4 is the default pick. If `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` or `FDB_LISTEN_IP` are set, they will _not_ be overwritten. Otherwise, the first IPv4 (or IPv6, depending) address returned by `hostname -I` is used. This is used because under some dual stack networking setups (especially under Podman, looking at you pasta), only the v4 address will be written to `/etc/hosts`. At this point, if `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` still isn't set, an error is thrown that no valid IP could be found. `hostname -I` doesn't output a stable order, but containers often will only have a single IP address. In a container connected to multiple networks, there isn't a sure way to figure out the correct public IP automatically, which is why `FDB_PUBLIC_IP` isn't overwritten. ## Enhanced FDB_COORDINATOR ip resolution ### Issue FDB Coordinator discovery always looks up IPv4 addresses, as `dig` by default searches for A records. It also doesn't respect the local `/etc/hosts` file. ### New Behavior Based on the value of `FDB_IP_VERSION`, fdb coordinator ip is discovered with either `getent ahostsv4` or `getent ahostsv6`. This will prefer the local hosts file if it has the name, otherwise it will try to reach a remote DNS server.

signal.title: BulkLoad: only require file containment for the range this fetchKeys owns
signal.text: A bulkload fetchKeys was rejecting the SST ingest fast path whenever any file in its task set fell outside the range being fetched, and falling back to key-value replay for the whole batch causing bulkload to take longer. The mismatch is structural, not a fault: two different range granularities meet in fetchKeys. bulkLoadFetchKeyValueFileToLoad builds localBulkLoadFileSets from the whole *task*, while `keys` is one destination shard piece. startMoveShards cuts the destination at pre-existing keyServers boundaries, so a task spanning several of them becomes several fetches -- and every one of those fetches is handed the task's entire file set, most of which belongs to the other pieces. Classifying all 3,428 mismatches on a 1B-key restore by how the offending file sits against the range being fetched: 87.0% no overlap 54.9% disjoint, 32.1% touching a boundary only 13.0% partial overlap 10.3% straddling an edge, 2.7% spanning it The 87% are not this fetch's files at all, so it can drop them and still ingest. Only the 13% are real conflicts -- ingesting those would write outside the range -- and they must still force the fallback. The all-or-nothing check was a deliberate guard, not an oversight: ingestSSTFiles was unfiltered, so ingesting a set containing unowned files would have written keys outside the shard. Fix the guard rather than remove it -- selectOwnedBulkLoadFileSets() keeps only the file sets whose range this fetch owns, and the fast path is then taken for those. Files that straddle or span a boundary still force the fallback, because ingesting them would write outside the range. selectOwnedBulkLoadFileSets() is pure and unit tested, including the exactly-once invariant: every file set must be claimed by exactly one fetch across the task's pieces, since dropping one silently loses data and duplicating one ingests the same keys twice. The test was confirmed red against the old behaviour (3 == 1). Measured effect on SSBulkLoadFileRangeMismatch at 100M scale: 342 before, then 85 and 199 in two later runs whose bulkload path was byte-identical. So the direction is established but the magnitude is not -- that counter has at least 2.3x run-to-run spread, driven by shard geometry rather than by this code. Also demote DDBulkLoadTaskFallbackToNormalDataMove from SevWarn to SevInfo. All 654 occurrences in the same run were Reason=PhaseMismatch on tasks already in phase Complete, at rebalance priorities 120 and 122 and never at the bulkload priority of 140. It is a benign race between a rebalance data move and task completion, not a bulkload fallback, and at SevWarn it was read as evidence of one. The attached task phase is deliberately not logged: it is a snapshot from when the task was Triggered/Running and can never show the Complete that caused the mismatch, which getBulkLoadTask already logs at SevWarn. ` 20260813-204050-stack_restore-bf06cb6ae1c0cb07 compressed=True data_size=38566706 duration=3617644 ended=100000 fail_fast=10 max_runs=100000 pass=100000 priority=100 remaining=0 runtime=0:27:55 sanity=False started=100000 stopped=20260813-210845 submitted=20260813-204050 timeout=5400 username=stack_restore`

signal.title: [release-7.4] Fix an old exclude failed bug
signal.text: Port apple/foundationdb#13645 to release-7.4. Problem: In removeKeysFromFailedServer, the writes that unassign a dropped shard from the dest servers (serverKeysFalse) and the writes that reassign it to the new team as an empty range were pushed into a single actors vector and awaited together. krmSetRangeCoalescing performs a read-modify-write on the serverKeys map, so when a server appears in both the dest set and the new team, running the two batches concurrently lets the coalescing reads observe stale state and produce an incorrect serverKeys assignment. Solution: await the unassign batch first, then run the empty-range assignment in a separate batch, ensuring the serverKey map assignment is correct. Same fix already backported to release-7.3 in apple/foundationdb#13662. release-7.4 still used the wait()/actor-compiler style rather than main's co_await, and shardId needed to become state since it now crosses the new wait() boundary -- same conflict resolution as the 7.3 backport. 100K: 20260813-171407-praza-port-7.4-pr13645-817f-e3951c728b485de6 pass=100000 fail=0 ended=100000 max_runs=100000

signal.text: ## Summary - Convert the seven remaining asynchronous Redwood tests from Flow actor syntax to C++ coroutines, remove the actor-compiler dependency, and rename `VersionedBTree.actor.cpp` to `VersionedBTree.cpp`. - Preserve extent-queue stream priority with `race(...)` and capture live B-tree progress counters by reference so the correctness test still terminates. - Keep the other nine synchronous tests and existing production implementation unchanged. ## Validation - `fdbserver_kvstore_test -f /redwood/correctness/btreeCloseWithQueuedCommits --seed 1` - `fdbserver_kvstore_test --simulation --seed 1` (4 tests passed) - Parameterized `fdbserver -r unittests` coverage for `Lredwood/correctness/btree`, `:/redwood/performance/extentQueue` with 2,048 entries, and `:/redwood/performance/set` - `clang-format --dry-run --Werror fdbserver/kvstore/VersionedBTree.cpp`
